The member sees a translated message asking them to print or export the document to a new PDF: from the API (api.pdf_active_content_refused, api.pdf_not_inspectable), on the React group files page (groups:files.upload_pdf_*, which previously showed only "Failed to upload file") and on the accessible group files page (govuk_alpha_groups.states.file-pdf-*). Other upload pages still show their existing generic error. Restricted-but-openable PDFs saved with compressed object streams (some bank statements, payslips and official forms) are refused as uncheckable, and fillable forms with a submit button are refused. Checked against 400 real PDFs with no false refusals. Pinned by tests/Laravel/Feature/Security/E086/F551ActivePdfUploadRefusedTest.php and F551PdfActiveContentInspectorTest.php. Files uploaded before this change are not re-scanned.

  • The React web server ran an out-of-date nginx (1.27.5) and printed its version on its own error pages (F-552, Medium; reported by Cyphere during the independent penetration test). The production image was built from nginx:alpine3.21, a tag that freezes nginx at 1.27.5, and nginx's built-in pages (for example the 410 returned for /wp-login.php) ended with nginx/1.27.5, on production and on the pen-test server. Both React Dockerfiles now build from nginx:1.30-alpine (the supported stable line, 1.30.5 today), both nginx configs set server_tokens off, and the four nginx test scripts use the same image so CI tests what ships. The deploy's Dockerfile sanity check (scripts/deploy/phases/validate-env.sh), which looked for the literal FROM nginx:alpine and would have stopped the next deploy, now accepts any Alpine-based nginx image, and a test pins the check and the Dockerfiles together. The deploy builds with --no-cache but not --pull, so later 1.30.x patch releases arrive only when the base image is pulled on the server. Pinned by tests/Laravel/Feature/Security/E086/F552ReactNginxVersionDisclosureTest.php.

  • High-risk staff actions now ask for a fresh authenticator code (E-085). Because staff can now remember a device, being signed in no longer proves the code was entered recently. Changing a role or sign-in email, granting super-admin, banning or deleting a member, setting someone's password, resetting their two-factor, signing in as a member, adjusting balances or granting credits, reversing an exchange, erasing via a GDPR request, managing enterprise roles, changing sign-in/SSO/API-key/secret settings and moving or purging communities are refused with AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED unless a code (or recovery code, passkey, or identity-provider sign-in) was entered in the last 15 minutes (5 for resetting someone's two-factor). The app asks for the code and repeats the action; one confirmation covers further high-risk actions for the next few minutes. A password alone, or a remembered device, is not accepted. New middleware step-up (App\Http\Middleware\RequireRecentSecondFactor); tests tests/Laravel/Feature/Security/TwoFactor/StaffStepUpTest.php and StaffRememberedDeviceTest.php.

  • A broker's report queue told them how many complaints were about them (F-549, Low). Reports a broker is part of are withheld from their queue (F-454), but the queue's total was only corrected for the page being shown, and the page's count boxes counted every report in the community. Either number, minus the reports the broker could actually open, was the number of complaints about them or their content. The rule now lives in one place (App\Services\ReportQueueVisibility) and the queue, its count boxes and the new dashboard card all count only what the broker can open. No report content or reporter identity was exposed. Regression test tests/Laravel/Feature/Security/E084/F549ReportQueueTotalTest.php.

  • A broker or coordinator whose account also carried an admin flag could change the broker panel's admin-only settings (F-548). The save for the broker Configuration page decided "admin" by its own check, which counted the flag whatever the role. Everywhere else the platform's single rule (AdminTier) treats brokers and coordinators as operational staff, never admins, even with the flag. The save now uses that rule, and the Configuration page locks the same settings for those accounts.

  • The code scanner (Semgrep) began blocking on two places that insert HTML into a page, the feed post renderer and the shared SafeHtml component, after an update to its online rules on 2026-10-03; neither file had changed. Both already pass the HTML through the platform's DOMPurify profile (sanitizeMemberRichText), and both findings had previously been reviewed and dismissed as false positives on GitHub. The reasoning is now recorded on the lines themselves (nosemgrep), which is what the blocking scan reads.

  • A new high-severity advisory in braces (CVE-2026-93687 / GHSA-vfj7-8cjw-p6xm, a stack-overflow denial of service from deeply nested patterns), published with no fixed version, is recorded as a time-limited exception for the mobile app and the accessible frontend (expires 2026-11-03). In both it is only ever run on the repository's own file patterns: in the mobile app by build and pre-commit tooling that does not ship in the app, and in the accessible frontend by a template file-watcher that is switched on only in development.

  • The person a concern note is about can no longer rewrite it (F-544). They could already neither read nor delete it, but they could overwrite its text or move it out of the concern category through the member-notes edit route. The edit is now refused, as the read and delete routes are, for the subject and for anyone they do not outrank.

  • The production settings file is now owner-only, and every deploy keeps it that way (F-541). /opt/nexus-php/.env holds every platform secret. It, and seven .env.bak-* copies holding older secrets, could be read by every account on the production server (mode 664/644). They were set to 600 by hand on 2 October 2026. A new deploy step, secure_env_file_permissions in scripts/deploy/phases/validate-env.sh, now runs before anything is built. It re-applies owner-only access to .env and every .env.bak-* copy, logs any file it had to tighten (never its contents), and stops the deploy if it cannot. This matters because a hand edit or a cp backup quietly reopens the file. A new CI test, scripts/test/test-env-file-permissions.sh, covers it in the Migration Safety Gate.

  • The monthly restore drill now proves the encrypted offsite copy, and reports every result. scripts/restore-drill.sh used to restore only the copy kept on the server and told nobody when it failed. It now downloads the newest encrypted database backup from the offsite remote, refuses one that is missing, more than three days old or not really encrypted, decrypts it with the drill's own key, restores it into a throwaway database and checks row counts and that the database's triggers and views came back. It also unlocks the uploaded-files, storage and server-configuration backups from the same night, checks each is a complete archive that actually holds files, and checks the configuration still carries the master key. It ignores sub-folders in the Drive folder, fails if it cannot read the live database to compare against, then deletes everything it downloaded. The monthly message lists the start of each key the backups are locked to, marked as owner key or server drill key, so the owner can see their own keys are still on the list. Pass or fail it sends a Telegram message; a drill that cannot send its message counts as failed. A lost or wrong key is therefore found within a month rather than during a disaster. DRILL_SOURCE=local keeps the old local-only drill for development. It also now reads database settings safely from an .env that has Windows line endings or both spellings of a setting (F-123, E-080).

  • Every deploy now installs the monthly restore drill's schedule. The drill's 04:00-on-the-1st schedule was only a comment in the script, and no deploy step installed it, so nothing guaranteed it ever ran. scripts/deploy/phases/install-backup-cron.sh now writes /etc/cron.d/nexus-restore-drill next to the nightly backup's cron file, re-asserting it on every deploy and correcting hand edits (F-123, E-080).

  • The Google Drive sign-in used for offsite backups is now limited to the backups it creates. scripts/setup-rclone-local.sh asked Google for access to the whole Drive; it now asks for drive.file (only files the backup tool itself created), refuses to continue with a wider token, and sends the server only that one connection instead of the whole local rclone configuration. scripts/setup-rclone-gdrive.sh installs rclone and age from Ubuntu's packages instead of piping a script from the internet into a root shell. It also no longer adds its own nightly schedule next to the one every deploy installs, which made two backups run at once; it removes that old entry, finishes by running one real backup and then the restore drill, and its printed restore help now describes the encrypted files. On Windows it now also finds rclone right after installing it through winget, which puts it in a versioned sub-folder the script did not look in. Takes effect only when the owner re-runs the sign-in (F-123, E-080).

  • New server step to set up backup encryption: scripts/setup-backup-encryption.sh. Run once as root on the server with the owner's two public keys. It generates the restore drill's own key (once, never replaced), writes the root-only list of public keys the backups are encrypted to, and stores the Telegram details for backup alerts. It refuses fewer than two owner keys, the same key twice, anything that is not an age public key, and any private key. scripts/setup-rclone-gdrive.sh now calls it before its test backup (F-123, E-080).

  • Two tools for the owner's own computer to make and test backup keys: scripts/backup-keygen.sh and scripts/backup-decrypt.sh. The first makes a key and shows the secret half, also in groups of four for a paper copy, plus the public half for the server; it can save a private copy (readable only by the owner). The second opens any downloaded backup file, or the small key-check file, with a key that is pasted, typed back in from paper (spaces and any case accepted) or read from a file. It says PASS or FAIL, never stores the key and never leaves a partial file. It only says the key does not open a file when that is what age reports; a damaged download or a failure to fetch the tool is reported as such, with age's own message, so a good key is never mistaken for a lost one. On Windows both run age in a throwaway Docker container, so nothing needs installing (F-123, E-080).

  • The backup encryption tests now run in CI. The Migration Safety Gate installs age and runs the six backup tests (nightly encryption, restore drill, cron install, server setup, owner key tools, Drive setup checks). The Drive setup check also had a flaw that could have let a "this must not be present" check pass when the forbidden text was present; fixed and confirmed against the old scripts (F-123, E-080).

  • The extra database backup taken during deploys no longer goes to Google Drive unencrypted, and no longer deletes other backups there. A deploy that changes the database makes its own backup first (scripts/deploy/lib/db-backup.sh). Unless an older encryption setting happened to be configured, that copy was uploaded to the same Drive folder as a readable file, and its clean-up deleted every file in the folder older than seven days, the nightly backups included. It now encrypts to the same keys as the nightly backup, skips the offsite copy rather than upload it readable, does not let a logging step hide a failed upload, and cleans up only its own files. The monthly restore drill now counts every unencrypted file still in the folder, whatever wrote it (F-123, E-080).

  • The nightly backup now also protects the server's master key, and no longer fails quietly. Some database fields (two-factor secrets, encrypted identity details, tokens) can only be read with the key in the server's .env, and no backup held it. The nightly job now uploads that file encrypted, as nexus_config_DATE.tar.gz.age, and keeps no unencrypted copy of it in the backups folder. It also: alerts on any failure anywhere in the job, not only the steps that were checked; gives files their real name only after they are verified, so a crash cannot leave a broken file that looks healthy; treats a missing Google Drive sign-in on the server as a failure rather than quietly skipping the offsite copy; refuses to back up a file store that does not exist or holds no files; and requires at least two of the owner's keys, no longer counting the server's own drill key, which would be lost with the server (F-123, E-080).

  • The nightly offsite backup copies are now encrypted before they leave the server. scripts/server-nightly-backup.sh encrypts the database, uploads and storage backups with age to every public key in a root-only recipients file on the server (at least two, so losing one key does not lose the backups) and uploads only the encrypted *.age files, plus a small key-check file the owner can open to prove a stored key still works. Missing keys, a single key, a missing age or a failed upload now stop the upload, exit with an error and send a Telegram alert (new scripts/backup-alert.sh, which reads its settings in a way that cannot silently lose them and treats a message Telegram rejects as not sent); there is no unencrypted fallback. The nightly job now also refuses a database dump that was cut short (no completion line) instead of keeping and uploading it, and any failure of the nightly job, not only the upload, sends a Telegram alert. Copies kept on the server stay unencrypted for fast restores. rclone sync of the whole backup folder is replaced by rclone copy of the encrypted files only, with offsite clean-up limited to those files. Needs the keys installed on the server before it is deployed, or the offsite copy stops (F-123, E-080).

  • Four platform-maintenance pages are now limited to god accounts. The test runner, sample-data generator, image converter and blog restore pages opened for any community administrator who typed their address, although they act on or report about the whole installation and the sample-data tool's own server check already required a platform administrator. They now use the same god-accounts-only guard as the cron jobs and performance pages (F-534).

  • Six old admin page addresses now forward to the current pages instead of bypassing their module checks. Old addresses for group types, group ranking, group locations, group geocoding and two smart-matching screens still opened pages directly, and because the admin area checks module switches by the start of the address, these older spellings skipped those checks. They now forward to the current page for each (group types, group ranking, the groups list, the broker match approvals, the matching analytics), which carries the normal check. None of them was linked from any menu (F-533).

  • The AI-agents admin pages now close when the AI-agents switch is off. The menu already hid them and the server already refused their requests, but typing a page address still opened an empty page whose every request failed. The pages now show the usual "not available" screen instead (F-532).

  • The older AI-agents admin tools now need both the AI-agents switch and the Caring Community switch. The older KI-Agenten admin page and its ten actions disagreed about which switch turned them on: the page followed the AI-agents switch, three actions followed the Caring Community switch, and the other seven, including approving the agents' suggestions one at a time or all at once, followed no switch at all. A community with both switched off could still apply agent suggestions. The page and every action now require both switches (F-531).

  • The Swiss data-protection (FADP) admin pages now stay closed unless the community has switched that module on. The module is off by default and the admin menu already hid it, but typing the page address still opened it, and the nine admin actions behind it (retention settings, the processing register, the consent ledger export and the disclosure pack) only checked that the caller was an administrator. The page and those actions now require the module to be switched on. Members' own consent records are unchanged (F-530).

  • Switching off the marketplace now also switches off coupon administration. The admin page for merchant coupons, and the three admin actions behind it (list, pause, delete), checked only the coupon switch and ignored the marketplace switch above it, so a community with the marketplace turned off could still manage coupons. Both the page and the actions now need both switches on, the same rule members and sellers already follow (F-529).

  • An account record can no longer leak private fields if it is ever turned into a response by mistake. The safety net that hides private account fields only covered the current password field. It now also hides the old password column still filled in for some older accounts, the password-reset token, and contact, location, payment and role details, so an accidental output elsewhere in the code cannot expose them (F-417).

  • The phone app's check that every outside link goes through its safe-link helper now looks at the whole app. The automated check only searched two folders, so four places that open web pages, in the payment and link-handling code, were outside its view. It now searches every folder except build output, and the places that legitimately open links themselves are named with the reason (F-480).

  • Links that open the phone app can no longer slip past its own safety checks. When the app could not match a link, or deliberately refused it, it still handed the original link to the app's screen router, so any web page, email or other app could open screens the checks were meant to keep closed. Refused and unrecognised links are now stopped, apart from the payment-return links members need. The check that keeps the in-app image viewer private could also be dodged by writing its name in capitals or with an encoded slash; it now compares names case-blind and after decoding (F-496, F-497).

  • A refusal from the platform's background-jobs button now carries a readable message instead of the number 400. Platform administrators have a page that lets them start one of the platform's routine background tasks by hand. If the task named does not exist, the refusal came back with the text the administrator had typed sitting in the slot reserved for the platform's own error name, and the number 400 sitting in the slot reserved for the message a person reads. Nothing unsafe happened — only platform administrators can reach the page, the refusal still refused, and nothing was displayed as a web page — but any tool reading the answer had no reliable way to tell one kind of refusal from another, and a person reading it was shown a number. The refusal now carries a proper error name and a readable message, matching the equivalent refusal on the scheduled-tasks page beside it. Starting a task that does exist is unchanged (F-470).

  • A sign-up addressed to a community the platform cannot identify is now refused instead of quietly creating the account in the main community. Apps and websites can tell the platform which community a visitor is in by sending its number. If that number arrived as something that is not a number at all — a community's short name typed into the wrong box, for example — the platform ignored it completely and fell back to the main community. Somebody signing up for their local timebank was therefore told "registration successful" while their account had actually been created somewhere else entirely. The same mistake made with an unrecognised number has always been refused; the unreadable value now gets the same refusal. Real community numbers, short names and community web addresses all still work exactly as before, and pages that name no community at all — the home page, sign-in, about — are untouched (F-479).

  • A community number with a decimal point or similar no longer gets quietly rounded down to a different community. The fix above refused values that are not numbers at all, but a value such as 1.9 or 1e0 still counts as a number to the software, which then chopped it down to a whole number — 1, the main community — so a sign-up sent that way was still created in the wrong place. Only a plain whole number is now accepted as a community number; anything else gets the same refusal as an unknown community. Ordinary community numbers, short names and web addresses work as before (F-504).

  • The "who has read the new policy" figures can no longer be pushed up by reloading a link, and no longer count reads that cannot have happened. Each policy email carries a tracking image and a tracking link. Every time either was fetched it was counted again, so one person reloading eight times showed as eight opens; reads were counted for emails that had not even been sent yet; and the automatic scan that many email security systems do the moment a message arrives was counted as the member reading it — which wrongly took that member off the list of people an administrator still needs to chase. Each recipient now counts once, only after their email has been sent, and not during the first two minutes when those automatic scans happen. Tampered links still record nothing. Separately, the "read the policy" button in these emails pointed at an address the server did not answer, so it led to an error page; it now opens the policy (F-469).

  • A broker can no longer close the safeguarding re-check about an administrator. When a community's safeguarding rules change, the platform raises a "please re-check this person's clearance" request for each affected account. Brokers could already not change an administrator's clearance decision itself, but they could still mark the re-check request about an administrator as done, so nobody was prompted to look again. Closing a re-check now follows the same rule as the decision: a broker may close one only for an ordinary member, administrators keep their full say, and nobody may close the one about themselves (F-502).

  • Removing a listing from a marketplace collection now says so when there was nothing to remove. Asking to take a listing out of one of your collections always answered "removed", even when that listing had never been in the collection — including a listing from another community. Nothing was ever changed or revealed, but anything relying on the answer was misled. It now answers "not found" in that case, the same way whether the listing exists elsewhere or not at all. Removing a listing that really is in your collection works as before (F-503).

  • Publishing a policy in a large community no longer holds up the administrator, or the policy itself, while every member's email is lined up. Publishing wrote one email record per member there and then, inside the administrator's own request and while holding a lock on the policy — in a big community that is thousands of rows before the page could answer. Now only the first 250 are written at that moment, saved together with the publication itself, and the rest are added in the background in batches. If that background step is ever lost, the regular email task notices and finishes it, so nobody is missed. Policies published before policy emails existed are never picked up by that catch-up, so they will not suddenly send emails (F-471).

  • Safeguarding alerts about a member now stop going to their old community once they have moved. When a platform administrator moved a member to a different community, the yearly safeguarding check-in and the safeguarding-clearance renewal alerts kept going to the old community's staff — naming the member and the kind of record — while the member's new community heard nothing. These alerts now only go out while the member still belongs to the community that holds the record (F-424).

  • The older partner time-credit transfer now re-checks everything at the moment the credits move. The original partner connection (switched off by default, and off on the live platform) checked the people, the partnership and the credit agreement first and then moved the credits a moment later without looking again. A change made in between — a member suspended or withdrawing consent, a partnership suspended — did not stop the transfer. It now re-checks all of these at the moment the credits move, exactly as the newer partner connection already does, and never credits an account that is no longer active (F-396).

  • The automatic check that stops published passwords from being built into setup scripts now checks every part of a script, not just the file as a whole. This check exists because a password published in the code once ended up on real accounts. It accepted a script as safe if a safety guard appeared anywhere in the file, so a script could guard one step and create an administrator account from a published password in another step that could be run on its own. Each step that creates a password must now be protected itself, or only be reachable through a protected step (F-494).

  • Three exceptions in the automatic security scan of the software the platform depends on now only cover the versions they were judged safe for. The scan stops a release if a dependency has a serious known weakness, and keeps a list of reviewed exceptions. Three of those exceptions applied to every version of their package, so if a later update had brought back a vulnerable version, the scan would have stayed silent. One now applies only to the fixed version and later, one only to the two versions actually reviewed, and one — for a package no longer used anywhere — has been removed, so it will be reported if it ever returns. A new automatic test keeps them this way (F-501).

  • Pages built with the page designer can no longer draw over the rest of the site. Community administrators can design public pages, and the designer already stripped the usual ways of making something cover the whole screen — but one more way still worked, and the app's own built-in styles offered another. Instead of chasing each one, a designed page now sits inside a frame that nothing inside it can draw outside of, so a page can never cover the site's header, menus or footer. Screen-size and feature conditions in a page's styles are also now checked before use, like the rest of its styles already were. Normal page designs look the same (F-499, F-500).

  • The security-scanning guide now shows exceptions limited to the versions that were actually checked. Its own example of how to write a dependency-scan exception used the "every version, for ever" form that F-501 found to be unsafe; the example and a short explanation now show the bounded form instead (F-501).

  • Caring-support hours can no longer pay a supporter whose account is suspended or banned. When a coordinator logs hours for a support relationship they can be approved and paid straight away. The platform already refused this if the organisation behind it was suspended, but it never checked the supporter, so a suspended or banned supporter was still paid. Logging such hours is now refused with a clear message, and nothing is recorded as approved. Supporters in good standing are paid exactly as before (F-505).

  • Settling a member's time-credit estate now pays only a beneficiary who can receive it, and can no longer make hours vanish. When an estate was settled in favour of a named person, the platform never checked that person's account, so a suspended or banned beneficiary was paid. Worse, if the beneficiary had since moved to another community, the hours were taken from the estate, paid to nobody, and the estate was still marked as settled. Settlement now checks the beneficiary first; if they cannot receive the hours, it is refused and the estate keeps them. Normal settlements are unchanged (F-506).

  • An administrator can no longer see or handle a volunteering safeguarding incident that is about them. The platform's other safeguarding records already keep people out of records about themselves, but the volunteering incident records did not: an administrator who was the subject of one could read the investigators' notes, rewrite them, assign the case to themselves and close it for good. Such incidents are now left out of their lists and treated as not found, they cannot be changed by that person, and nobody can assign an incident to the person it is about. Every other administrator handles these incidents as before (F-507).

  • Staff alerts now reach every administrator, however their access was granted. Administrators are now normally set up with an administrator setting rather than an "administrator" job title, but five kinds of alert still looked only at the job title: reported content, exchanges waiting for approval and disputes, new groups, new members waiting to be approved, and completed identity checks. In a community whose administrators were all set up the newer way, those alerts reached nobody. They now use the platform's single shared definition of who should be told, so administrators and brokers receive them as intended, and ordinary members still do not (F-508).

  • A member's personal-data download no longer includes the safeguarding officer's private notes about their vetting. Everywhere else, the platform deliberately shows a member only the outcome of their safeguarding clearance — the decision and its dates — and keeps the officer's private notes, internal summary, the reason given and who decided out of view. The personal-data download did not follow that rule and included all of them. It now matches: members still receive their own clearance decision, its dates and which clearance it is (F-509).

  • Someone signed in to a community that has since been renamed is no longer shut out of every page. When a community's short name changes, apps and the accessible website can go on sending the old one for a while. Since the refusal above and its sister fix, sending a name the platform no longer recognises refused the request outright — even for a member who was signed in and whose own sign-in clearly said which community they belong to. Those members are now simply served their own community. Nothing is relaxed for a visitor who is not signed in: an unrecognised community name from someone with no account is refused exactly as before, and a signed-in member naming a different real community is still refused (F-481).

  • The "Maximum transfer" limit an administrator sets now actually applies. The System Config page offers a cap on the largest number of hours one member can send another in a single transfer. It saved, it showed the saved value back, and it did nothing: the platform read a different setting, so the real ceiling stayed at the built-in 1,000 hours. An administrator who capped transfers at five hours would still have seen a member move two hundred in one go. The page now writes the setting the platform reads. Transfers below the cap are unaffected, and a community that has set no cap keeps the same built-in ceiling it had before (F-492).

  • Switching a part of the platform off for a whole community is now recorded. Administrators can switch off messages, the wallet, listings and five other areas for everyone in their community. Neither of the two pages that can do it kept any record of who did it or when — the matching record for the other kind of switch on the very same page was added earlier and did not cover these. Both pages now write the same entry, naming the administrator, the area and whether it was switched on or off. What administrators are allowed to do has not changed (F-493).

  • Reordering a community's safeguarding questions is now recorded. Staff can change the order the safeguarding questions appear in. Creating, editing, deleting and importing those questions have all recorded who did it since an earlier fix; reordering was missed and left no trace at all. It now leaves the same kind of entry. Reordering only changes what order things are shown in and cannot add or remove any protection — this is about being able to answer "who changed this, and when" (F-495).

  • A transfer from an outside organisation is no longer reported back to them as having failed when it actually went through. Time credits arriving from another platform are added to the member's balance first, and the member is then emailed about it. If that email could not be sent, the platform told the sending organisation the whole request had failed — using the exact answer it reserves for "try this again". A sender that did try again, with a new reference, would have paid the member twice. One everyday reason the email could not be sent was the member's own choice to receive no federation email, which was then recorded as an email system fault rather than as the member's decision. The sender is now told the transfer was accepted, with the notification problem reported alongside it. The failure is still recorded on the transfer and still shows on the email-delivery page administrators use, and a repeat of the same transfer still re-sends the missed email without paying anyone twice. Connections to outside platforms are switched off by default and none is connected today (F-422).

  • When an outside organisation takes back time credits it sent you, your wallet now shows it. Hours delivered from another platform were listed in the wallet while they stood, but the moment the sender cancelled them the entry was hidden — so the balance dropped by five hours and there was nothing anywhere on the member's history to explain where they had gone. No local record of either the arrival or the removal was ever kept. A cancelled delivery now stays on the wallet and reads as hours leaving the account, matching the drop. A delivery the platform could not take back, because the hours had already been spent, also stays visible and still reads as hours received, because the member kept them. Ordinary deliveries are shown exactly as before. Connections to outside platforms are switched off by default and none is connected today (F-491, first half; the second half — how much a cancellation is allowed to take when the hours have been spent — is unfinished and needs a decision from the platform owner).

  • An outside organisation can no longer leave a review on a member who never agreed to federated reviews. A member chooses whether to take part in federation at all, and separately whether reviews from other communities may appear on their profile. The older partner interface has always checked both before accepting a review from outside; the webhook route checked neither, so a partner could put a review on the profile of someone who had never opted in, and it counted towards their public rating. The webhook now asks the same two questions. A member who has opted in is reviewed as before, and the rule added earlier — that a review must describe a real exchange with that member — still applies on top. Note what is still not possible: a member cannot refuse one particular reviewer on another platform, because the platform holds no reliable identity for a person it does not host. The choice is all-or-nothing for the member, and suspending the partner for an administrator. Connections to outside platforms are switched off by default and none is connected today (F-406, remaining half).

  • An outside organisation can no longer pay time credits into the wallet of a member who turned federation off. Every member has two switches: whether they take part in federation at all, and whether they accept time credits from other communities. Both are off until the member turns them on. Every other way an outside platform can send time credits reads those switches first and refuses — the webhook route, the one most likely to be used in practice, never looked at them, so credits from an outside organisation landed in the wallet of someone who had refused federation, and a community using those switches as a safeguarding control did not have one. The webhook now asks the same question the other routes ask. A member who has opted in is paid exactly as before, and a repeat of a transfer that was already accepted still gets the same "already recorded" answer rather than a false failure. Connections to outside platforms are switched off by default and none is connected today (F-484).

  • A copy of your data no longer includes the staff notes about a safeguarding concern you raised. When someone asks for a copy of everything the platform holds about them, the file they got back included, for any safeguarding concern they had reported, what staff had decided to do about it and the notes they wrote when closing it. Those notes are about the person the concern was about, not about the person who raised it, and the website itself has always kept them hidden from the reporter. The download now shows exactly what the website shows: your own account of what you reported, when, how serious you said it was and what state it is in. Staff looking into a concern still see their full record, and the rest of the data copy is unchanged (F-488).

  • A refused safeguarding-training decision now stays on the community's record after the member deletes their account. If staff turned down someone's safeguarding training certificate and that person then deleted their account, the refusal disappeared with them — who refused it, when, and why. The community was left with no record that it had ever happened. The same thing was fixed earlier for refused background checks, for the same reason, and this closes the matching gap. The refusal itself is kept; everything the member submitted alongside it — the course name, the provider, the certificate reference and any document link — is still erased, and training the member submitted that nobody refused is still deleted in full (F-489).

  • The accessible version of the site now works out who is an administrator the same way the rest of the platform does. It had a staff-only door that decided by reading a single text label on the account. Most administrator ranks are not stored in that label — they are stored as separate yes/no settings — and the information it was reading did not include the label at all, so the door would have turned away everyone, including genuine administrators. Nothing was affected in practice: the door is not attached to any page today. It now asks the platform for the account's actual rank, admits community, network and platform administrators, and still turns away brokers, coordinators and ordinary members (F-498).

  • Switching off a safeguarding requirement across listings is now recorded. A maintenance command clears the old "background check required" marker from listings, and with one option it does that for every community at once. It left no record at all — nobody could afterwards be told who ran it, when, which communities it covered, or how many listings lost the requirement. The command now asks whoever runs it to name themselves, refuses to run if the record cannot be written, and writes two entries: one before it changes anything, so a run that stops half way still leaves proof it happened, and one afterwards with the numbers. This matches the change made to the related clean-up command, so both show up in the same place. The checks that already stopped an accidental run are unchanged (F-427).

  • A safeguarding clearance brought over from the old records now says which check it is for. Communities can import historic background-check decisions into the new safeguarding system. Those imported clearances were stored without recording the type of check behind them, so a broker looking at the vetting list saw a confirmed clearance with nothing beside it saying what had actually been checked. Every clearance a member of staff records by hand has always carried that detail. Imported ones now carry it too, taken from the community's own configured checking scheme, and the import refuses to create a clearance it cannot name rather than creating a blank one (F-426).

  • A first-aid certificate is no longer relabelled as a criminal-record check when deleting its file fails. If a member deleted a volunteering credential and the stored file could not be removed, the platform kept the record as a marker so the leftover file is not forgotten about — but that marker alone made the record show up in the member's own list as retired criminal-record evidence, with the wrong name against it. A first-aid or food-hygiene certificate is not a criminal-record check, whatever went wrong with the file. Those records now keep their own name and appear in the "needs review" group instead, so the unfinished clean-up is still visible. The file itself is still withheld, because the member asked for it to be deleted, and genuine criminal-record records are still handled exactly as before (F-425).

  • A broker who has been reviewed can no longer remove other members' comments on that review. Brokers help moderate comments, and the only thing stopping them clearing up criticism of themselves was a rule about comments they had written. A review is written by one member about another, so a broker the review was about could delete or hide every comment other members had left on it — and a hidden comment disappears for everyone. The equivalent buttons on the community feed were corrected earlier; the comment moderation screen was missed, on both the delete and the hide. Both now refuse a broker who is the subject of the review. Moderating comments on anyone else's review, and everything administrators can do, is unchanged (F-420).

  • A broker can no longer cancel an administrator's safeguarding clearance. Brokers are trusted to record and withdraw the safeguarding checks of ordinary members, and the only thing stopping them was a rule that said they could not do it to themselves. Nothing stopped a broker doing it to an administrator. In a community that only lets vetted people contact a safeguarded member, a broker could therefore take an administrator's clearance away and cut them off from the very members that protection exists for, with the administrator recorded as having been withdrawn by the broker. A broker may now only record or withdraw a clearance for someone they are senior to, which is the same rule already used when staff adjust another person's time balance or suspend an account. Administrators are unaffected and can still do this for each other, brokers can still do it for ordinary members, and the existing refusal to decide your own clearance is unchanged (F-421).

  • Approving volunteered hours no longer pays time credits into a suspended or banned account. Approving hours creates brand-new time credits — nobody's wallet is reduced to pay for them — so the credits were new money in the community, and they were landing on accounts an administrator had deliberately barred. All four places that approve hours were affected: the organisation's own approval screen, the automatic approval that some communities use, the community administrator's approval page, and the caring-community review decision. Each of them already refused to pay out on behalf of a suspended organisation but none of them looked at the member. All four now apply the same platform-wide rule every other way of paying a member already applies. The hours stay waiting rather than being marked approved and unpaid, so they can be approved normally the moment the suspension is lifted — nothing is lost. Approving an active member's hours, and declining anyone's, are unchanged (F-475).

  • Settling a group exchange now checks everyone's account again, and can no longer make time credits disappear. A group exchange checked that a member's account was in good standing when they joined and never looked again, even though settlement can happen days later. Two things went wrong because of that. A member suspended or barred in the meantime was still paid. And if a member had been moved to a different community in the meantime, the hours were taken off the people receiving the service but never reached the person who provided it — the exchange was marked finished, a wallet record was written for a payment that had not happened, and four hours simply vanished from the community's total. Settlement now re-reads every participant's account at the moment the hours move, and refuses outright if the credit cannot land, so either everything moves or nothing does. A refused settlement changes no balance and leaves the exchange ready to finish as soon as the account is in good standing again. Ordinary settlements are unchanged (F-476).

  • The caring-community review decision no longer pays out on behalf of an organisation that is suspended or was never approved. Three other places that approve volunteered hours already refused to create time credits for an organisation a community had suspended or had not yet approved. This fourth one — the caring-community coordinator's review decision — never looked at the organisation at all. Approving there created brand-new time credits for the member and pushed the organisation's own balance into the red, with a payment record to match, for an organisation with no standing to pay anyone. It now applies the same rule as the other three, both before the decision is made and again at the moment the credits would move. Declining hours is still allowed while an organisation is suspended, so a coordinator can clear the queue, and an approved organisation is unaffected (F-478).

  • Taking back a network-administrator privilege now really takes it back, whichever button granted it. Two of the four ways to appoint a network administrator — "move and promote", and a bulk move with the promote option ticked — recorded the appointment in two places at once, while removing it only cleared one of them. The account kept full administrator powers in a community that never appointed it, including reading the member list with everyone's email addresses, while the panel, the button and the audit entry all said the privilege had been removed. The other two ways were corrected earlier; these two now match them. Appointing a network administrator still works exactly as before (F-464).

  • A data-protection request from a member now always reaches somebody. When a member asks to see, move or erase their data, the platform alerts the community's administrators. The list of who to alert was built the wrong way, so in a community whose administrators were appointed the normal way it could reach nobody at all — no alert on the bell, no push, no email — and the request would only surface weeks later through a nightly overdue check, close to the legal deadline. The same fault silently skipped the alerts for new listings, new community events, new volunteering opportunities, and the message telling a community that another community had accepted its partnership request — so those went unseen too. Eight places that pick administrators were corrected to match the one that was already right. Nobody who should not be alerted now is (F-490).

  • A safeguarding case can now be given to a network administrator, and they appear on the administrator list. Someone who runs a community and the communities under it could not be named as the person responsible for a safeguarding incident or for a volunteering organisation. The request was simply refused and the incident was left with nobody responsible for it. The same account was also missing from the administrator list the member-records screen shows, so no work could be routed to them there. Ordinary members still cannot be given a safeguarding case, and the administrator list still does not include brokers (F-467).

  • An administrator can no longer delete the concern note recorded about themselves. Staff can record a confidential concern about a member or about another member of staff. A recent fix stopped the person a concern is about from reading it — but the delete button was never checked, so they could still destroy it without ever seeing it. Deleting a concern note about yourself, or about someone at or above your own level, is now refused, and the note survives. Anyone senior enough to see the note can still remove it, and ordinary notes are unaffected (F-462).

  • Network administrators can now use three controls they were being refused. The platform records an administrator's authority in two ways, and three checks only looked at one of them. A network administrator — someone who runs a community and the communities under it — could not send or clear a community emergency alert, could not open a job applicant's CV, and could not read the view and like figures for a post. The emergency-alert case was the worst: the account was let through the admin door and then turned away by the page itself. All three now use the platform's single, canonical test for who is an administrator. Ordinary members and brokers are still refused all three (F-466).

  • An outside platform can no longer create unlimited time credit in a community. The older partner interface capped a single transfer at 100 hours and then only checked that a credit agreement existed with the other community — it never read the monthly limit written on that agreement. Because the sender is on the other platform there is nothing to take the hours out of locally, so the credit was made from nothing: against a published limit of 10 hours a month, ten calls put 1,000 hours into the community. The month's running total is now checked against the agreement before any credit is added, and where the agreement states no figure, 200 hours a month applies. Cancelling a transfer does not hand the budget back. The same transfer also used to be recorded as if a named local member had sent it, so that member's wallet showed hours they had never spent; a transfer from an outside platform is now recorded with no local sender at all. Connections to outside platforms are switched off by default and none is connected today (F-440).

  • An outside platform can no longer publish reviews on a member it has had no exchange with. The older partner interface accepted a review with no checks whatsoever — no exchange behind it, no limit on how many, no check that the two people named had ever dealt with each other — and wrote it straight in as approved and publicly counted, in the name of a real member of the community who had not written it. Five identical one-star reviews could be planted on any member, and they moved that member's public rating. A review arriving this way must now name a real exchange in that community that both named people took part in, and one exchange can earn only one review. This brings the partner route in line with the rule the platform's own review screen has always applied. Connections to outside platforms are switched off by default and none is connected today (F-441).

  • An outside platform can no longer read private messages it was not part of. The message-reading route for partner platforms filtered only on the community the credential belonged to — which, for an outside platform, is the whole community — so any partner credential could read the full subject and body of every message any other partner had delivered, a hundred at a time. It was reading more than the member it belonged to can: a member's own inbox does not show these messages at all. A partner may now read only the messages it delivered itself. A partner reading back its own correspondence is unaffected (F-446).

  • The older partner interface now honours the two privacy switches a member sets on their federation profile. "Share my location" and "Share my skills" are both off unless a member turns them on, and every other part of the platform respected that — but the partner routes returned a member's home address and skills regardless, for the whole membership, 100 at a time. All three affected routes (the member list, a member's profile, and a listing's owner details) now withhold both fields when the member has them switched off, and a member can no longer be found by searching on a field they have hidden. A member who chooses to share still shares (F-447).

  • An outside platform can no longer send a message in the name of a real member of your community. The older partner interface deliberately skips checking the sender, because on a genuine partner transfer the sender is on the other platform — but it then stored whichever local member the partner named as the author. The message landed in the member's inbox, was recorded twice under that name, and the platform emailed it out with that member's real name in the subject line, the preview and the "From" panel, carrying whatever text the partner had written. A message arriving from an outside platform is now stored with no local author; the sender's name as the partner supplied it is what identifies them, which is what the alert and the federation inbox already showed. The same check on the internal route, which does refuse this, is unchanged (F-448).

  • One partner platform can no longer block another's transfers. Transfers from partner platforms are de-duplicated by a reference the sending platform chooses, and every partner of a community was sharing one pool of those references — so the first platform to use a given reference owned it permanently, and a second platform's genuine transfer was turned away as a duplicate before any of the money checks ran. The member it was meant for was never credited, and because "duplicate" is the one answer a well-behaved sender does not retry, the transfer simply vanished. Each partner platform now has its own pool. A platform repeating its own reference is still correctly refused and the member is still credited exactly once (F-450).

  • A key issued for an outside organisation is now recorded as belonging to one. When a community creates a partner key it can link that key to the outside organisation it is for. The link was saved, but the key was still filed as if it belonged to another community on this platform — and the partner routes read that to decide what to serve. The result was that a key made for an outside organisation was answered with other communities' members instead of the issuing community's own, and several protections written specially for outside organisations never ran on any key the platform could actually make. A key linked to an outside organisation is now recorded as one. Keys made without that link are unchanged, and the check that the organisation belongs to your own community still applies. Note this fixes what new keys are recorded as; keys already in the database are unchanged and need a decision from the platform owner. Connections to outside platforms are switched off by default and none is connected today (F-463).

  • A partner key can no longer be handed your own members' private federated correspondence. The message-reading route for partner platforms has two paths. One was corrected earlier so an outside organisation reads only the messages it delivered itself. The other path — the one every key the platform could actually make was taking — simply returned every federated message involving anyone in the community that issued the key, subject and full text, including their exchanges with a third community. It was showing more than the members themselves can see: these messages do not appear in a member's own inbox. A key that names no outside organisation is party to nothing, so it now reads nothing. A key linked to an outside organisation still reads back the messages that organisation delivered (F-468).

  • The partner member directory no longer publishes barred, suspended and refused accounts. The rule excluding accounts that are not in good standing sat on one of the two paths only, and it was not the path any real key took. So a partner key could list — 100 at a time, and look up by name — the profiles of people a community had banned or suspended, people whose registration an administrator had refused, and people who never confirmed their email address. The same gap meant such an account could still be sent a message and still be credited with time credits through the partner route. All four places now apply the same rule the rest of the platform applies. Active members are listed, reachable and payable exactly as before (F-483).

  • A member's hidden skills can no longer be confirmed by guessing at them. A member can switch off sharing their skills with partner communities, and the partner directory correctly leaves the field blank. But the search box still matched against it: searching for the exact hidden wording brought the member back and the result count said "1", confirming the guess without ever showing the value. The search box now ignores a skills entry the member has switched off, which is what the platform's own federated search already did and what the matching filters were corrected to do earlier. A member who chooses to share is still found by their skills and still has them shown (F-465).

  • Taking back a network-administrator or platform-administrator grant now really takes it back. Granting either of those did two things at once: it set the permission, and it also changed the person's listed role to "administrator". Taking the grant back only undid the first, so an ordinary member who had been granted and then un-granted was left as a full community administrator — able to manage every member — while the panel, the button and the audit entry all said the permission had been removed. Granting now sets the permission alone, which is all it ever needed to do and is exactly what the super-admin panel's own version of the same grant already did, so granting and un-granting now cancel each other out exactly. Someone who was already an administrator before the grant stays one, as they should (F-431).

  • Editing a network administrator's phone number no longer takes away their permissions. A recent fix made the two member-edit screens switch off administrator permissions whenever the role was set to something ordinary. That fired too widely: for an account listed as an ordinary member who had been given network-administrator permission — the normal result of granting it from the super-admin panel — every save switched the permission off, including a save that only changed a phone number. The community could lose its only network administrator through routine admin work, silently, and the account could not restore itself. Permissions are now only switched off when the operator actually changes the role to a lower one. Genuinely demoting someone still removes every permission, on both screens (F-452).

  • Approving people in bulk no longer demotes them. The bulk approval button set everyone it approved to "member", whatever they already were, so approving a pending broker or administrator quietly stripped their role. On an account that also held a separate administrator permission, the effect was worse: the record was written down to "member" while the permission stayed on, so the person still had powers the screen said they had lost. Bulk approval now leaves the role alone, exactly as approving one person at a time already did (F-429).

  • Moving someone to another community no longer carries their administrator powers with them. Moving an account only changed which community it belonged to. An administrator of community A, moved into community B, arrived administering B — appointed by nobody there — and a network administrator moved between two networks kept that permission, which silently re-pointed their reach at the new network's communities. Community-level authority (the administrator role and both community permissions) is now cleared on every move, including the bulk move, and the record of the move now says what was removed instead of only where the person went. Platform-wide access is left alone, because it is not a permission over the community the person happens to sit in. The separate "move and promote" action still promotes, as intended (F-453).

  • A member of staff can no longer read the monitoring record kept about their own messages. Messages are copied for review when someone is being watched, and the broker screens let the person a copy was about open it — so they could read that they were being watched and why, how serious it had been judged, the reviewing administrator's private note and that administrator's name, and the decision later filed about them. Those screens now refuse when the record is about the person asking, and the review queue and the archive list leave their own rows out, so the record cannot be reached by paging through a list instead. The same refusal now covers the exchange detail screen, which handed a member of staff who was one of the two people in the exchange the other member's email address and the internal risk note an administrator had written about their own listing. Reading records about other members is completely unchanged (F-436).

  • A member of staff can no longer read a complaint made about them, or about something they posted. The moderation screens showed the name of the member who complained, their picture, and the complaint in their own words — to the very person being complained about, who as a broker holds moderation powers over them. The complaint screen now refuses, and the moderation queue leaves those complaints out, so one cannot be found by paging through the list instead. This brings the moderation screens in line with what the platform already does elsewhere: a seller told their marketplace listing has been reported is never shown who reported it or what they wrote. Closing or dismissing such a complaint was already refused. Administrators are unaffected, and staff reading complaints about other members see exactly what they did before (F-454).

  • Nobody can now read the private safeguarding notes written about their own vetting record. Brokers are allowed into the vetting screens as part of their job, and those screens accepted any member's identifier — including the reader's own. The person the record was about could therefore read the safeguarding officer's private note and the private summary of what they had been cleared for (both of which are deliberately stored scrambled precisely because they are sensitive), the internal code giving the reason a clearance had been withdrawn, and the name of the officer who decided their case. Those four details are now left out when the record is about the person reading it. They can still see their own clearance status and dates, which is what the member's own "my vetting status" page has always shown. Opening another member's record is completely unchanged (F-437).

  • The private notes staff keep about a person's conduct are no longer shown to that person, whatever their role. These "concern" notes were already hidden from brokers, but the rule stopped short of administrators — so a community administrator was served the full text of a concern that a senior platform administrator had recorded about them, along with the name of the colleague who wrote it. The rule now applies at every level: you are never shown a concern note about yourself or about someone at your own level, while anyone senior to the person the note is about still sees it in full. It also now covers three more places the same notes were being read: the activity timeline, the spreadsheet download, and the response returned after editing a note. Ordinary CRM work is unaffected — staff still read concern notes about the members they support (F-457).

  • The safeguarding review queue no longer shows a member of staff the monitoring record kept about their own messages. Messages are copied for review when someone is being watched, and the queue listed every copy in the community with no exception for the person reading it — so the subject of the monitoring could see, in their own work screen, that they were being watched, the reason recorded, how serious it had been judged, the reviewer's private note and that reviewer's name. Their own copies are now left out of the queue, and out of its count, so they cannot be reached by turning to another page. Copies about other members are unchanged, and colleagues still see the record about the person in question — it is hidden only from that person (F-455).

  • Nobody can now open the safeguarding history kept about themselves. The per-member safeguarding history screen, and its spreadsheet download, accepted any member's identifier including the reader's own. Because every opening of that screen is itself recorded, and the record names who opened it, an administrator could read the list of colleagues who had looked at their own safeguarding history and when — and see that their own messages were being copied for review, and why. Oversight stops working when the person being overseen can watch it happening. Both the screen and the download now refuse, and refusing leaves no entry in the history. Reading another member's history, on either route, is unchanged, and a supported member can still see the notes recorded on their own support arrangement (F-456).

  • Changing a safeguarding question to "information only" can no longer quietly cancel the protection members chose. Each safeguarding question a community asks has a type: a tick box, a drop-down, or a plain information note. Changing a live tick box into an information note left every member's answer on record, left the question switched on and left its protections in place — but the platform stopped counting those answers. A member who had said "I will only deal with vetted people" became contactable by anyone, was not told, and stopped seeing their own choice in their settings. Brokers could do this as well as administrators. The platform already refused to switch such a question off or to strip its protections; it now refuses a change of type as well, whenever that change would stop any member's live answer counting. Changing the type when nobody's answer would stop counting, or when nobody has a live answer, still works exactly as before (F-433).

  • Changes to a community's safeguarding questions now record who made them. Creating, editing or removing a safeguarding question, and applying a country's safeguarding preset, were each recorded with the time, the network address and the browser used — but with no account against them. "Who changed this safeguarding setting?" could not be answered from the platform's own records, which is also what would have made the problem above hard to trace after the event. All four now name the member of staff who acted. Members' own actions were already recorded correctly and are unchanged (F-434).

  • Dependencies: the markdown renderer (league/commonmark) is updated to 2.10.3, which closes a way of slipping disallowed raw HTML past its sanitiser when a disallowed tag name ends the literal (GHSA-97jj-33gv-5xf9). The platform renders member-written text through this library, so the fix matters beyond the dependency graph. Lockfile-only; no code change.

  • A safeguarding alert raised when the deadline sweep runs in a community with the module switched off now opens a single grouped report rather than two, and a per-community failure is reported the same way. A partner review is also now checked against the safeguarding rules before anything else, so if those rules cannot be read the partner is told to try again rather than being given a refusal that looks final (follow-ups to F-406 and F-408).

  • Demoting an administrator now actually removes their powers. Changing someone's role back to "member" in the admin panel recorded the demotion and showed them as an ordinary member, but left their administrator permissions switched on underneath — so they could still view any member's account as that member, and at platform level still see every community on the installation. Both admin screens are fixed, including the one the super-admin panel actually uses. Removing "god" access still has no control anywhere on the platform and is deliberately unchanged (F-399, F-400).

  • A member of staff who is also someone's supporter can no longer confirm their own request on that person's behalf. Where a supporter prepares an action and the supported member approves it, a staff account that was itself the supporter could record that approval as having been given "offline" — moving the supported member's time credits with no act of consent by them anywhere in the record. Staff who are not involved can still confirm by phone or in person for someone who cannot use the platform themselves, and members can still confirm their own (F-405).

  • A community administrator can no longer switch off the automatic safeguarding deadline alert for concerns that are already open. Turning off the caring-community module, or marking the community inactive, used to stop the alert immediately and silently: a concern stayed open, sat past its review deadline, and nobody was told. The check is now driven by the overdue concerns themselves, so neither switch can reach it, and if it ever does escalate a concern in a community with the module switched off, that is raised as an alert naming the community. Changing any community feature is also now recorded in the administrator audit log, which it previously was not (F-408).

  • Destroying legacy vetting evidence now leaves a permanent record. The maintenance command that deletes old criminal-record-check files and clears the details from the records wrote nothing anywhere — there was no way afterwards to say who ran it, when, for which community, under whose data-protection approval, or how much was destroyed, and the approval reference the command insisted on was thrown away. Every run now writes two entries to the data-protection audit log, one before anything is touched and one with the results, both naming the operator and the approval reference. The operator must now name themselves, and if the record cannot be written the command refuses to destroy anything. This command is run by hand on the server and is not reachable from the website (F-409).

  • The one-off import of old vetting decisions no longer grants a safeguarding clearance to someone whose later check did not pass. It looked only at the old approved record and never at the rest of that member's history, so a member whose most recent criminal-record check had been refused or withdrawn was given the platform's confirmation that they were cleared to contact members who had asked for safeguarding protection. Any contradicting record now sends the member to the broker review queue instead, which grants nothing — the route the import was always meant to use for unclear cases. This import is run by hand on the server and is not reachable from the website (F-410).

  • A partner platform in another community can no longer leave reviews on a member it has had no exchange with. A review arriving from a partner must now name a completed exchange that partner recorded with that member, one exchange can earn only one review, and a partner is limited to five reviews of the same member a day. Previously a partner could publish any number of approved one-star reviews, with its own wording, on any member of the community, and they counted towards that member's public rating. Connections to outside platforms are switched off by default and none is connected today (F-406).

  • Time credit arriving from an outside platform is now limited to what the community has agreed to accept. Each transfer was already capped at 24 hours, but nothing limited the total, so the same request repeated under a new reference could create unlimited credit. A community must now have an active credit agreement, and the month's total is checked against it before any credit is added — the same rule the other three partner protocols already follow. Where the agreement states no figure, 200 hours a month applies. Connections to outside platforms are switched off by default and none is connected today (F-407).

  • An outside platform can no longer hand itself back the monthly credit limit it has just used up. The limit above counted only transfers still marked "completed" — but the same outside platform decides when a transfer stops being completed. It can cancel one at any time, and if the member has already spent the credit nothing is taken back: the transfer is simply marked as disputed and the member keeps the hours. Either way the hours stopped counting, so the month's allowance was free again and the same trick could be repeated without end. In testing, 72 hours were delivered into a community whose agreement allowed 30, with the running total reading zero at the finish. Every hour that arrives from outside now counts towards the month whatever happens to it afterwards, which is what the other partner routes already do. The trade-off is deliberate and worth stating: a partner that cancels a transfer in good faith does not get that part of its allowance back until the following month. Cancelling a transfer still takes the credit back from the member when they still hold it. Connections to outside platforms are switched off by default and none is connected today (F-428).

  • A broker can no longer change or delete their own insurance certificate. Two ways of doing that were missed when the rest of this was fixed: moving the expiry date out (or clearing it) made an out-of-date certificate count as current again, so the insurance requirement an administrator had placed on the broker's own listing stopped applying; deleting the record erased an administrator's refusal of that insurance. Administrators are unaffected, and a broker can still manage other members' certificates (F-401).

  • A member of staff can no longer close the safeguarding re-check about themselves. A community asks for these re-checks automatically when it changes its safeguarding policy, and until now the person the re-check was about could mark it handled — so nobody was prompted to look at their clearance again, and the record named them as the person who dealt with it. Confirming and withdrawing a clearance already refused this. Closing somebody else's re-check is unchanged (F-402).

  • A member of staff can no longer sign off the monitoring record of their own message. Messages are copied for review because someone is being watched; marking a copy reviewed, approving and filing it, or flagging it all took it out of the staff review queues and made it eligible for automatic deletion — and the person doing it could be the sender or the recipient. All three actions now refuse the people the message is between, at every level of staff. Reviewing other members' copies is unchanged (F-403).

  • The same refusal now applies on the safeguarding screen, which reaches the same message copies by a different route and so was not covered by the change above (F-404).

  • The demo-data seeding commands no longer carry a password in their source, and refuse to run outside a development environment. A command that creates sample accounts held its shared password as plain text in this repository and had no environment check at all — it would seed those accounts into whichever community it was pointed at. The password has been removed from every seeder, the value now comes from an environment variable or is generated for the run, and all of the seeding entry points now refuse to run unless the environment is explicitly one of local, development or testing. The previous checks were written the other way round — they refused only an environment named exactly production, so an unset or differently-named environment passed straight through. The affected accounts on the live platform had their credentials rotated at the same time; none of them had ever been signed into. A new blocking check, npm run check:seed-credentials, fails the build if a credential literal or an unguarded seeder reappears (F-398).

Developer-tool copies of brace-expansion in the root, react-frontend and web-uk lockfiles are updated to patched releases (GHSA-q2hr-2g5m-vwhr, Dependabot #145/#150/#151/#158–#160); none ships in a production image. Lockfile-only; no code change.

  • Submitting the same caring-support visit twice at the same moment (for example a double-click) can no longer record and pay it twice (F-391).

  • A broker who has been reviewed can no longer hide or delete that review from the community feed. Deleting it that way also deleted other members' comments on the review; the review-moderation page already refused this (F-390).

  • A broker can no longer clear the compliance controls an administrator placed on the broker's own listing: they cannot record or verify their own insurance certificate, or change or remove the risk tag on their own listing. An insurance certificate recorded as already verified now also records who verified it (F-389).

  • A group marked private or secret is no longer sent to external partner platforms, and neither is who joins it. A group made private after being shared is withdrawn from them without its details. External partner connections are switched off by default and none is connected today (F-386).

  • An administrator of one community is no longer treated as an administrator of every other community when member profiles are shown. This could not be reached through the platform today, but would have exposed members' exact locations and surnames to other communities' administrators if a profile page were ever opened to signed-out visitors (F-394).

  • When a podcast creator deletes their own account, the complaints other members made about their episodes, and the moderators' decisions on them, are now kept. Previously the account deletion removed them along with the episodes (F-383).

  • A club organiser importing members from a spreadsheet can no longer create accounts that skip the community's identity check. Imported accounts now follow the same joining rule as accounts an administrator creates: where the community requires an identity check, the account waits for it (F-382).

  • Blocking a member of a partner community no longer reveals the name and photo of someone who has not chosen to be visible to other communities. Only members who have joined cross-community sharing, in a partnership that is active, can be blocked across communities, and the block list names them only while they stay visible (F-381).

  • A web address typed into the platform — an interview link, an evidence link, an order tracking link, a venue website — can no longer be written in a form that sends whoever clicks it to an unrelated website. One shared safety check covers all of these, and it had a gap (F-380).

  • If a supported member revokes their carer while a payment by that carer is already in progress, the payment is now refused instead of completing (F-342).

  • A member who has opted out of cross-community sharing can no longer use any of the cross-community connection features — sending, accepting, rejecting or removing a connection, or checking its status (F-373).

Previously those connections stayed, the other community kept reading your name and photo, and turning the setting off also removed your ability to delete them (F-352).

The record previously said the action was taken by "System".
