  • "Clear all communities' cache" now clears every community. It used to clear only the first five, while telling the admin it had cleared them all (F-287).

  • The admin fraud-alert count now shows the open alerts on the Fraud Alerts screen. It was always zero before (F-318).

  • Members who switch notification emails off no longer get emails when someone likes, comments on, replies to or shares their content (F-317).

  • If a message's community has been removed before the safeguarding review check runs, the check is now skipped instead of running against another community's records (F-288).

  • Members can now block someone from a partner community. The block stops that person's messages, connection requests and credit transfers, and the emails and notifications they would send, in both directions, and removes any connection between the two. Blocked partner-community members appear in your blocked list, and their profile page has a Block button. Blocks made in the past that never took effect across communities now do (F-284).

  • Opening an unsubscribe link in an email no longer switches your emails off by itself: it now asks you to confirm with a button. Email security scanners that open links automatically were turning people's notifications off without them knowing (F-321).

  • Reviews of an employer now follow the employer's "who can see my profile" setting, as other reviews already do (F-286).

  • The public version page no longer shows the server's PHP version or the text of the latest change, which named the security fix it contained. It still shows the version identifier the deploy tools rely on (F-314).

  • Thumbnails can no longer be made from files in private upload folders, such as message attachments and voice messages, that the web server already refuses to serve (F-290).

  • Asking for your account to be deleted through the data-protection request form now needs your password and signs you out everywhere, the same as the other two ways of deleting an account (F-308).

  • Rejecting or cancelling a data-protection request now records who did it, when and why, and adds an entry to the audit log, as completing one already did (F-325).

  • A visitor filling in the sales enquiry form can no longer slip a second email address into the reply-to line of the email the sales team receives (F-323).

  • Two parts of the standard email layout, the statistic-card icon and the badge colour, are now checked before they go into an email. Nothing uses them unsafely today; this closes the door before anything does (F-322).

  • A record that does not say which community it belongs to is now refused by the database instead of being filed under the platform's main community (or under none). On 29 tables — including reviews, comments, likes, badges, group posts and memberships, connections, event replies, polls and volunteering — a missing community used to be filled in silently, which is how some TimeBank Ireland reviews, a group post, a volunteer application and badges ended up in the wrong community earlier this year. Records that name their community are unaffected (F-328, O-087).

  • Joining a community through its own sign-in provider (for example a council's staff login) now follows that community's joining rules. An invitation-only or closed community no longer admits anyone the provider knows, and a community that requires approval or an ID check now holds the new account for that step instead of letting the person straight in (F-270).

  • A broker can no longer approve or reactivate a member whose identity check is still outstanding or has failed; only an administrator can release those accounts. Brokers still approve ordinary sign-ups and lift ordinary suspensions (F-277).

  • "Report a problem" no longer records the part of the web address after ? or #, where sign-in and password-reset links carry their codes, so those codes can no longer end up in the staff support queue or in error reporting. The platform also strips them from reports sent by older versions of the app (F-281).

  • A custom page made with the page builder can no longer contain a form that sends what visitors type to another website; a form on a community page can only send to that community's own site. Pages saved earlier with such a form are made safe when they are shown (F-282).

  • Text a member types when declining or cancelling an exchange, and members' names, can no longer put a working link or other hidden code into the email the other member receives; they now appear as plain text (F-273).

  • A community's email sender name or address can no longer be used to add hidden recipients, such as a secret Bcc, to the emails that community sends, including password resets. The email settings page now refuses such values with a clear message (F-280).

  • A blocked member can no longer peer-endorse the person who blocked them. Peer endorsements now also follow the safeguarding contact rules and the member's "who can see my profile" setting (F-271).

  • Employer reviews now follow the same rules as other reviews: a blocked member cannot leave one, the safeguarding contact rules apply, and a member can leave one review per employer instead of an unlimited number (F-272).

  • Blocking someone now also stops them rating your exchanges, marketplace orders or volunteering, commenting on your ideas, and reacting to your podcast episodes. None of these can email the person who blocked them any more (F-279).

  • A member who has been moved to a different community can block people again. Before, the screen said the block worked but nothing was stored, and the blocked person's messages still arrived (F-285).

  • Deleting a member's account now also takes them off the community's newsletter list and removes any newsletters still waiting to go to them. It no longer deletes the record that stops email reaching an address that bounced or opted out, so that protection survives the deletion (F-274).

  • Deleting a member's account now also removes their two-factor backup codes, which used to keep working, and their linked sign-in accounts, which held their real email address from the sign-in provider (F-275).

  • A data-protection request (such as a request to delete an account) can now only be set to one of its real statuses. Before, an unknown status was accepted and silently stored as blank, which took the request off the overdue alarm while the person's data was never deleted (F-324).

  • A legal document (such as terms of use) that has been published or agreed to by members can no longer be deleted, because deleting it wiped every member's record of having agreed. The admin screen now says, in the admin's own language, to switch the document off instead. Draft documents can still be deleted, and each deletion is now recorded in the audit log (F-276).

  • Switching a community's maintenance mode on or off now refreshes only that community's search-engine pages. It used to restart page rendering for every community on the platform (F-245).

  • The volunteering accessibility page now says truthfully that these notes are private and are not shared with organisations or coordinators, and a save that fails is reported as an error instead of "saved" (F-227).

  • "Add someone who can help" in linked-account settings now does what it says: the person you name is asked to help you, and nothing changes until they accept. It used to make you their helper instead (F-224).

  • The Caring Community "Verified" and "Coordinator" trust levels now require a real ID check. Email verification or a failed ID attempt no longer counts, and community settings can no longer remove the requirement (F-269).

  • Sending regional points now asks you to pick the recipient by name and confirm "Send … to …?" before anything is sent, and points can only go to active members of your community. Spending regional points in the marketplace is switched off until a checkout that honours the discount exists, so points can no longer be spent on a discount that never applied (F-225).

  • Every GitHub Actions step used by the build and release pipeline is now pinned to an exact, reviewed version, so a changed or hijacked tag upstream cannot alter what runs (F-008).

  • The Warmth Pass now says "Identity verified" only for members who have passed an ID check, no longer describes itself as proof a member is verified, and "Areas I help with" now lists help the member gives rather than help they receive (F-228).

  • A member's linked community sign-in now works only through the same sign-in system it was linked under. If a community admin later points the provider somewhere else, linked members have to link it again from their settings, so the change cannot be used to sign in as them (F-268).

  • Added an optional safeguard so that visitor addresses forwarded by Cloudflare are trusted only when the request comes through this platform's own Cloudflare account. It is off until the operator configures it, and changes nothing until then (F-248).

  • A job candidate's data export still includes the employer's notes about their application and interviews, but no longer identifies which staff member wrote the decision or proposed the interview (F-261).

  • A sign-in provider set up by a community admin can no longer sign someone into an existing account just because the email address matches. New members can still join through it, and anyone already linked keeps signing in. Providers approved by the platform operator are unchanged (F-244).

  • A community's donation and premium payments can now only go to the Stripe account created through that community's own Stripe setup on this platform. Another account entered by hand is refused, and one saved earlier is no longer used; payments fall back to the platform account until the community completes its own setup (F-263).

  • Brokers and coordinators no longer see staff concern notes written about themselves, about fellow brokers or about admins; they still see concern notes about ordinary members. Admins are unchanged (F-252).

  • Switching a module on or off from the System Config page is now recorded, like it already was from the other settings page. There are two admin pages that switch the same modules, and only one of them wrote a line in the admin record saying who had made the change and when. So an administrator could switch off the Caring Community module — the one that carries safeguarding — and nothing showed who had done it. That matters, because switching that module off hides every open safeguarding concern from the staff responsible for them. Both pages now write the same record, in the same form, so they cannot be told apart afterwards. Nothing about who is allowed to make the change has altered (F-460).

  • Switching Federation off on the System Config page now really switches it off. Federation is how a community shares things with other communities. Switching it off on that page only changed what members saw: the community looked un-federated, while it carried on sharing its listings, messages, transactions, member profile updates, groups, connections, reviews and volunteering opportunities outward, and carried on accepting other communities as partners. The switch on the other settings page had always done both halves; this one now does too, and switching Federation back on from the same page restores it properly. In practice the sharing that was continuing is between communities on this installation — sharing with outside platforms has been switched off since July and no outside platform is connected — and that is exactly the sharing an administrator would be switching off (F-461).

  • An outside platform's access key can no longer be swapped for a pass that skips the second check it was meant to require. A community can mark a partner platform's key as one that must sign every request it sends, using a second secret the partner keeps separately — so having the key alone is deliberately not enough to get in, and a key on its own is refused. But the same key could be handed to the sign-in endpoint and traded for an hour-long pass that needed no signature at all, carrying everything the key was allowed to do. A key that had leaked on its own was therefore as good as the full credential. That trade is now refused, and a pass already issued stops working the moment a community turns request signing on. Keys that do not require signing are unaffected and work exactly as before. Nothing had this setting switched on, so nothing was exposed by it in practice — the protection would simply have failed silently the first time it was used (F-449).

  • "Require member approval" and "require email verification" now actually do what the switch says. These two decide whether someone who signs up is held for a person to check, or is let straight in with the community's starting time credits. The settings page saved them under one name while the sign-up and sign-in checks read another, and most communities had a value stored under the name the checks read — so an administrator could turn member approval back on, see the page confirm it, reload and see it on, and the next stranger to sign up would still be let in and credited automatically. The same split made the switch inert in the other direction too: turning the requirement off did nothing. Both names are now written together every time either is saved, so the page and the platform can never disagree again. For communities where the two names were left saying different things in the past, the platform now takes the cautious reading and screens the new member; one save from the settings page sets it to whatever the community actually wants (F-458).

  • Finishing an exchange no longer pays time credits into a suspended or banned account. Every other way of moving credits to a member — a transfer, a donation, a grant from the community fund, a marketplace sale — already refuses to pay an account the community has suspended or banned. Finishing an exchange was the one way that did not, so a member an administrator had suspended for abuse carried on earning from exchanges, and the community's obligation to honour those hours carried on growing. It did not even need the suspended member to sign in: the other member confirming the hours had the same effect. Confirmation is now refused with a clear message, no credits move in either direction, and the exchange stays where it was — so the moment the suspension is lifted, either member can confirm it and it finishes normally (F-442).

  • The public list of categories no longer publishes every column the platform stores against them. The address that hands a website or app a community's list of categories — used by the listings, events, volunteering and search pages, and open to anyone without signing in — returned each category exactly as it is stored, whatever that happened to be. The categories table carries four columns that do not belong to it, evidently left behind by an old change applied to the wrong table, and one of them is named reset_token. All four are empty on every community, so nothing has been given away; the problem is that the address published whatever the table held, so anything added to that table in future would go out to the internet without anyone changing any code. It now sends a named list of details only — the category's identifier, name, web-address name, kind, colour, parent, position and whether it is switched on — which is everything the website, the accessible site and the phone app actually read (F-438).

  • The check that is meant to stop a password ever being published again can no longer be switched off by accident. Yesterday a shared password sat in this public repository for 153 days, and 22 accounts on the live platform accepted it. The automatic check added in response asked whether a piece of code mentioned the safety guard — not whether it actually used it. So a single unused line naming the guard, which does nothing at all when the code runs, was enough to make the check pass a seeding script that created a full platform-administrator account from a published password. The check also only looked in two folders, and not at the database update scripts, which are the ones that run against the live platform on every release. It now looks for the guard being genuinely used, treats a guard whose refusal is thrown away as no guard, and reads the database update scripts, the older update scripts and the start-up code as well. It still passes quietly on the honest code already in the repository, which was measured rather than assumed, and a new set of tests keeps both halves of that honest (F-430).

  • The phone app now checks every web address it hands to the phone, with no exceptions left. The app has one place that decides whether an address is safe to open — it refuses anything that could run code or pretend to be a file — and five screens were opening addresses themselves instead: the two marketplace payment screens, seller payment set-up, identity verification, and the "you must update" screen. Nothing unsafe could reach them (the payment addresses come from Stripe and the update address from the platform's own settings), so nothing was at risk; this closes the gap before it can become one, and each screen keeps the specific message it already showed when an address would not open (F-445).

  • Someone the community has formally refused can no longer be paid time credits. The platform keeps one list of account states that must never receive credits, and every way of paying a member is supposed to read it. The list was wrong in two ways: it named a state an account can never actually be in, so that entry protected nothing, and it left out "refused" — the state an account is put in when a community turns down someone's application to join. A refused applicant could therefore still be paid by a transfer, a donation, a grant from the community fund, finishing an exchange, a marketplace sale or a community delivery, and the credits were then stranded, because that account cannot sign in. Three of those six places had also written out their own copy of the list instead of reading the shared one, so the same two mistakes were repeated in each; all three now read the shared list, so it cannot drift again. Paying an ordinary member, and paying a newly registered member who has not yet confirmed their email address, are both unchanged (F-477).

  • Suspending a member now stops a payment that is already under way. A transfer and a donation both checked whether the recipient was allowed to receive credits, but they checked it a moment before the money actually moved and never looked again. If an administrator suspended or banned that account in the gap — a fraction of a second, but a real one, and we have reproduced it — the hours were still paid in. That is the opposite of what suspending someone is for, and the sender's hours were lost with it, because nobody can spend from a suspended account. Both now re-check the recipient at the moment the money moves, holding the account open so the answer cannot change underneath them, which is how the community fund and the marketplace delivery payout have always done it. Nothing is paid and nothing is taken from the sender when the recipient is refused. Ordinary transfers and donations between members in good standing are unchanged, including when something else about the recipient's account is edited at the same moment (F-411).

  • Blocking someone now stops a payment they have already started sending you. A transfer or a donation carries a note the sender writes, and that note is delivered to the recipient as an alert, a phone notification and an email — which is why the platform refuses one from someone you have blocked. That refusal was decided a moment before the credits moved and never looked at again, so a block made in the gap did not stop the delivery: the hours arrived and the sender's text arrived with them. We had suspected this and had not proved it; we have now reproduced it, on both the transfer and the donation. Both now re-check the block, and the community's safeguarding contact rules, at the moment the money moves. Blocking a different member, and ordinary transfers and donations between members who have not blocked each other, are unchanged (F-412).

  • A new member's welcome time credits can no longer be taken away by another member. Communities can give every new member a starting balance of time credits — five hours by default. To make sure nobody is paid twice, the platform checked whether a credit had "already been given" partly by looking at the wording on past entries in the member's wallet history. But the wording on an ordinary transfer between members is free text, written by whoever sent it. So any signed-in member could send a new member one hundredth of a credit, type the right words in the note, and the new member's welcome credits were never paid — permanently, silently, and repeatable against every new member. The administrator's screen simply reported nothing awarded. The platform now identifies a genuine welcome grant by something only the platform itself writes, so no member can imitate one. Members who were given their welcome credits under the old system are still correctly recognised and are not paid twice (F-474).

  • Removing a story from a highlight now tells you whether it was actually removed. A member can group their stories into highlights on their profile. Asking to take a story out of a highlight always answered "removed", even when that story was not in the highlight at all — someone else's story, a story from another community, or an identifier belonging to nothing. Nothing was ever taken from anyone else: the platform only ever looks inside the member's own highlight. What was wrong was the answer, so neither the member nor anything keeping a record could tell a real removal from one that did nothing. The answer is now "not found" when nothing was removed, and that answer is deliberately word-for-word the same whatever the identifier really was, so it still cannot be used to work out whether somebody else's story exists. Removing a story that really is in your own highlight is unchanged (F-418).

  • Deleting a community's single sign-on provider no longer records a deletion that did not happen. An administrator asking to delete a sign-on provider was told "deleted" even when their community had no provider by that name — including when the name belonged to another community — and the platform wrote that deletion into the administrator audit log, naming the provider. Nothing was ever deleted from another community; the problem was the record, and this platform's security assurance rests on that record being true. The request is now refused when there is nothing to delete, nothing is written to the audit log, and the refusal reads the same whether the name belongs to another community or to nobody. A real deletion still works and is still recorded exactly once (F-472).

  • Removing a member's verification badge now refuses a member of another community. An administrator of one community could ask to remove a verification badge from a member of a different community and was answered with an ordinary success. Nothing was ever removed — the platform only ever touches badges in the administrator's own community — but an operator, or any automated process driving this address, was told the removal had succeeded. The equivalent "read this member's badges" screen next to it was already refusing the same request outright; the two now agree. Granting and removing badges for your own community's members is unchanged (F-473).

  • Eight administrator actions no longer report success for something belonging to another community. Editing a newsletter template, deleting a role, setting which groups are in a collection, deleting a community-partner link, deleting a course category, deleting a skill category, switching off an emergency alert, and saving an internal note on a pilot enquiry each answered with an ordinary success when the thing named belonged to a different community. In every case nothing was changed — the platform's own checks stop at the community boundary — but the screen, and any automated process driving these addresses, was told the change had been made. The group-collection one was the worst: it also wrote an entry into the administrative audit log describing a change to the other community's collection that never occurred. All eight now answer "not found", and the group-collection entry is no longer written. One sibling action in the same file, deleting a newsletter template, already did this correctly and is what the others now copy. Administrators acting on their own community's records are unchanged (F-482).

  • Turning federation off now stops your listings being sent to outside platforms. Every way an outside platform can ask to see a member's listings already checked whether that member had agreed to federation at all, and refused if they had not. The outbound half — where the platform volunteers a listing to each connected platform as it is created or edited — never asked. It also left the per-listing "share with other platforms" marker switched on when a member turned federation off, so the next time they edited an old listing its title, description and their member number went out to every connected platform, after they had withdrawn consent. The outbound half now asks the same question as everything else, and turning federation off switches those markers off at the same moment. A member who has agreed to federation still has their listings shared exactly as before (F-413).

  • Un-sharing, closing or deleting a listing now tells outside platforms to drop it. A listing already sent to another platform stayed on display there for ever: stopping sharing, closing the listing or deleting it sent nothing at all, so the member saw it disappear from their own community while it carried on being shown elsewhere. The platform now sends a withdrawal message, using the same approach already used for volunteering opportunities. The withdrawal carries only enough to identify the listing — never the title or description again. A listing that was never shared still sends nothing (F-414).

  • A member who turned federation off is no longer alerted by an outside platform. Turning federation off already stopped the emails. The bell alert and the phone notification for the same two events — someone on another platform asking to connect, and a review arriving from another platform — were decided by a different switch that turning federation off never touches, so those members went on being alerted. Both now ask exactly the same question the email already asked. Members who have federation switched on are alerted exactly as before (F-419).

  • A request to erase someone's data from an outside platform is no longer recorded as done when it failed. When a member deletes their account or withdraws from federation, the platform tells every connected outside platform to erase the copy it holds. If that platform was down or refused, the instruction was dropped in silence: the retries the platform promises — after five minutes, half an hour, and two hours — never ran, and the alert that asks an operator to do it by hand never fired. A refusal now does fail properly, so the retries happen and an operator is alerted if they all fail. A refusal caused by federation being switched off, or by the outside platform having been suspended here, is recorded loudly instead of retried, because retrying could not reach anyone (F-485).

  • A completed transfer to an outside platform is now actually sent to them. When a member sent time credits to someone on another platform, the step that notifies that platform looked for the partner's identity in a place the record does not keep it, found nothing, and quietly did nothing — on every transfer, ever. The member's hours moved locally, and the receiving platform was never told, so the two sets of books drifted apart with no warning. The platform now reads the partner from where it genuinely records it. A transfer between communities on this platform is still never sent outside, even where the two use the same internal numbering (F-486). Connections to outside platforms are switched off by default and none is connected today.

  • A community can no longer be shown another community's transfer because two reference numbers happened to match. When a community sends time credits to an outside platform, the record keeps the outside platform's reference number in the same box that an ordinary community-to-community transfer uses for the receiving community's number. Both numbering schemes start at one and count up, so they overlap. A community whose own number happened to match an outside platform's number was served the other community's transfer when it asked for it by reference: the number of hours, the sending member's own written note, and that member's name. The platform now only treats that box as a receiving community when the transfer is demonstrably not one sent outside. Where it cannot tell, it refuses — a deliberate choice, because the alternative is showing one community another community's private transfer. A community reading its own transfer, whether it sent it or received it, is unaffected (F-487). Connections to outside platforms are switched off by default and none is connected today.

  • An outside platform that has been suspended can no longer switch itself back on, or wipe the record of why it was suspended. Suspending a connection is the only lever an operator has against an outside platform that is misbehaving. The step that handles a "partnership activated" message would have lifted that suspension on the outside platform's own say-so, and cleared the error count and the recorded reason along with it. Nothing could reach that step in practice — the two doors into it already turn away a suspended platform — but the step itself is available to any future code that forgets to check, so it now refuses. The error count and the reason are also no longer cleared by any message from the outside platform: only an operator, or a successful sync, clears them. Activating a connection that is genuinely waiting to be set up still works, and both doors still turn a suspended platform away (F-423).

Fixed

  • The admin GDPR dashboard now shows a real compliance score instead of 0. Since the page was rebuilt in April 2026 the server never sent the score, the consent coverage figure, the completed-requests count or the requests-by-type breakdown, and the page showed each missing figure as zero — so every community saw a compliance score of 0 and consent coverage of 0% whatever its actual position. The score is now calculated from three parts: data requests answered within 30 days (40 points; a closed request with no recorded closing date is not counted as on time), the share of members who have accepted every required consent at its current version (30 points; administrators are left out, as in the legal-document figures), and the share of recorded breaches that are resolved (30 points). "Completed this month" now shows this month's figure rather than nothing, a figure that fails to load shows "N/A" rather than 0, and the separate back-up calculation the server fell back to on error — which used different field names the page could not read — has been removed. A test now checks that the server sends every field the page reads.

  • The admin Group Recommendations page now shows the recommendations members are actually given. Since it was built in February 2026 the page read from a database table that has never existed; the error was silently hidden, so it always showed 0 recommendations, an average score of 0.00, a 0% join rate and "No recommendations found". It now reads the store the platform really fills when it works out which groups to suggest to each member (hour-timebank had 2,679 on 1 October), shows each one's score, whether the member has since joined, and the overall join rate, and reports a real error if that read fails. The average match score is now shown as a percentage, like the per-row scores. A regression test seeds real recommendations and checks the figures, including that one community never sees another's.

  • Chrome no longer types the admin's saved email into the admin sidebar search, or their saved password into secret fields. Admin pages with a hidden-text field — an AI provider API key, SMTP password, OAuth client secret, map API key, or a new password set for another member — looked like a sign-in form to the browser's password manager, so it filled the admin's own saved password into that field and their email into the nearest text box above it, which is the sidebar search. Pressing Save on such a page could then store the admin's login password as the API key or secret. Two earlier fixes only marked the search box, which Chrome ignores for saved sign-ins; all 20 such fields now use one shared component that tells Chrome, 1Password, LastPass and Bitwarden not to fill them, and a test fails if a new one is added without it.

  • The admin Cron Jobs page now shows whether each job's last run worked, and a failed run is no longer hidden. Every job showed "Last Status: Unknown", because the status label had no entry for the word the system records for a successful run ("success"). Worse, the page counted a run as failed only when it was recorded as "failed" — but the system records a failure as "error" — so a broken job showed no red mark and the "Last Failed" total stayed at 0. Both words now have translated labels in all eleven languages, and a job whose last run errored is marked and counted as a failure.

  • The pre-deploy check no longer counts a test suite as passed when part of it never ran. The PHP and React test suites are split into shards that run side by side. If a newer push cancelled some shards part-way, the check that decides whether a commit may be deployed still treated the suite as passed as long as the other shards had succeeded — on 30 September it accepted a run where two of the ten PHP shards had never run. Such a run is now not counted at all, so the check looks further back for a complete run, or refuses. A failed shard still refuses as before, including when it caused its siblings to be cancelled. A regression test now runs in CI on every push.

  • The new policy email screens and messages are now available in all eleven languages, not English only, and the policy email activity page shows each delivery state (queued, submitted, blocked, and so on) as a translated label instead of the raw system word.

  • Policy publication now rejects a missing change summary in the service itself, queues recipients in batches, and orders the email audit by publication time while preserving the title used when each notice was sent. The policy activity page also sets a proper browser title.

  • Legal document creation and settings now show the API's translated error explanation instead of a generic "Save failed" message, including when a document of the selected type already exists for the community. The automatic admin translation check now records, at both places, that these explanations are already translated by the server, which it had refused to accept without that note.

  • Network administrators can now use six screens that were wrongly refusing them. A network administrator is someone given authority over a community and the communities under it. The super-admin panel has always granted that as a permission on its own, leaving the person's listed role as "member" — and six places checked the listed role and nothing else, so they turned a real network administrator away. The six: seeing unpublished knowledge-base articles in the list, opening an unpublished article by link or by name, editing a shared resource someone else uploaded, deleting one, and running volunteer check-in for a shift. All six now ask the platform's single authority check, the same one the rest of the admin screens use. Nobody gains anything: an ordinary member is still refused at all six, and brokers and coordinators are still refused exactly where they were before. This was found while fixing F-431, which makes every network-administrator grant look this way (F-431 follow-up).

  • Saved-search alerts now count only the listings you can actually open, arrive in your own language, and stop for a suspended account. The hourly "new listings match your saved search" alert counted every listing, including ones a moderator had rejected, ones still waiting to be reviewed, and ones that had been erased. So a member could be told four listings matched and find one when they followed the link, and the platform was announcing content it had decided that member may not see. The alert now uses the same visibility rule as every other place listings are shown, and the number recorded against the saved search matches it. The wording of the alert was also written into the code in English, so it reached everyone in English whatever language they had chosen; it now uses the platform's translations and is written in the recipient's own language, in all eleven. And the alert is no longer sent to an account the community has suspended, banned or deleted. A member in good standing with a genuinely new listing still gets the alert exactly as before. While fixing this, the hourly task was also made to put the community setting back the way it found it when it finishes (F-435).

  • Six of the permissions a partner platform can be given now actually exist to give. When a community creates an access key for a partner platform it chooses what that key may do. The list of choices had fallen behind the platform: six permissions the partner routes check for — reading the list of communities, reading listings, reading and sending messages, and reading and writing reviews — could not be picked at all, so six documented partner features were unusable with any key the platform itself could create. The list of choices and the permissions the routes enforce now come from one place, and an automatic check fails if the two ever drift apart again. Of the six, sending messages, writing reviews and reading messages can only be granted by a platform administrator, not by a community's own administrator, in line with how moving time credits is already treated. Making up a permission that does not exist is still refused (F-451).

  • Tooling: js-yaml is now declared in the root devDependencies. scripts/preflight.mjs and the deploy check gate scripts/predeploy-ci-verify.mjs both require() it, but it was only named in overrides, so it resolved only while a stray copy sat in node_modules; any npm update/npm ci at the root removed it and both scripts crashed with "Cannot find module js-yaml" — for the deploy gate, a refusal indistinguishable from "not checked". Same class of fault as the undeclared minimatch fixed in 9794618e1.

  • Three places where an action was stopped because of a block now say "not allowed" rather than "bad request". The action was refused either way; only the explanation was wrong (F-336 follow-up).

  • Submitting a community survey response, or an emergency alert, with something missing now returns a clear message about what is missing instead of a server error (F-372).

  • Pausing or resuming an achievement campaign no longer shows an error; the pause or resume always worked, but the screen said it had failed.

  • Uploading a photo or file larger than 1 MB works again on every community's website. Since 24 September the web server in front of the platform refused any upload over 1 MB before it reached the platform, so an ordinary phone photo could not become a profile picture — which also stopped new members finishing the welcome steps. The web server now accepts uploads up to 105 MB, the same limit the platform itself uses, and each kind of upload keeps its own size limit.

  • "Was this article helpful?" answers in the Help Centre are now kept with the community whose article was rated. Every community's answers were being filed under the platform's main community.

  • The "Restrict matching" and "Require coordinator approval" safeguarding options now apply to matches. A match involving a member who chose either option, or who is under monitoring, is no longer shown or emailed to anyone until a coordinator approves it on the Match Approvals page. That page was always empty until now, because nothing ever sent matches to it. When a coordinator approves a match, both members are told. A rejected match stays hidden, and neither member is told. The matching screens and Help Centre articles are updated in all languages.

  • The post-deploy check of what search engines see no longer reports freshly re-rendered pages as frozen: it now judges a page by when it was last rendered, not by how old the code is. Deploys also no longer re-render dozens of existing pages at random because of a faulty "already exists" check.

  • Completing an exchange now earns experience points (XP) for both members. Until now a completed exchange earned nothing, because the XP award only ran for direct wallet transfers. Each member now receives the existing "complete a transaction" award once per exchange; no XP amounts or level thresholds were changed.

  • The mobile navigation menu no longer answers with a server error. The address that gives a phone app a community's simplified menu failed for every caller, signed in or not. The platform's built-in fallback menus are written into the code rather than stored in the database, so their entries have no database identifier — and the menu code insisted on reading one, which turned into an error the moment it looked. It now copes with an entry that has no identifier, and the address returns the menu it was always meant to return. As well as leaving apps without a menu, the constant failure was noise in the platform's error reports that could hide a real fault (F-439).

  • Signing up to a community that no longer exists no longer creates the account in the platform's main community. The phone app and the accessible website both name the community they are asking about by its short name. When that name matched nothing — because the community had been renamed or removed — the platform quietly fell back to the main community instead of saying so: the person was told "registration successful", was placed in a community they had not chosen, and was invisible to the community they meant to join. Reading anything that way was answered with the main community's details too. An unrecognised community name is now refused. The two other ways of naming a community, by web address and by the ?slug= setting, already refused it. Naming a community that does exist is unchanged, and a request that names no community at all — the platform's own home, sign-in and about pages — still reaches the main community exactly as before (F-443).

  • A refusal to serve a community now reaches the browser as a refusal, with its own reason and the usual protective headers. When the platform turned a request away because the community was unknown, was switched off, or did not match the sign-in being used, it wrote the refusal straight out and stopped the request there — before the step that adds the security headers, and before the step that lets a browser read an error coming from another address. A browser therefore reported an unexplained connection failure instead of the real reason, and the "community unavailable" page went out with none of the usual protections against being framed or mis-read. Each of those refusals is now an ordinary response, so it carries those headers and keeps its own status and reason instead of all three collapsing into one generic message. No member information was exposed by this (F-444).
